The Cenozoic Era. Stretching from sixty-six million years ago to the present day, this is the "Age of Mammals," spanning the recovery from the extinction event that killed the dinosaurs through the rise of primates, ungulates, carnivores, and ultimately humans. The era includes three major periods: the Paleogene, Neogene, and Quaternary. Climate shifted from greenhouse to icehouse conditions, and grasslands expanded, reshaping the course of evolution. The name means "recent life" in Greek.

Mammals radiated explosively after dinosaurs vanished, filling ecological niches left empty and diversifying into the major modern lineages—primates, carnivores, cetaceans, ungulates, and rodents. Flowering plants continued their dominance, including the evolution of grasses, which created vast savannas and prairies by the Neogene. Primates evolved during the early Cenozoic in tropical forests, eventually giving rise to apes and hominins in Africa.

Climate cooling intensified through the Cenozoic, culminating in ice ages and glacial cycles during the Quaternary Period—the last two point six million years. The Paleocene, Eocene, and Oligocene epochs of the Paleogene saw early mammal diversification and the establishment of modern mammalian orders. Humans, the genus Homo, emerged only in the last three million years, representing just a tiny fraction of the Cenozoic's vast span.

The Cenozoic Era follows the Cretaceous Period, the final age of dinosaurs, and its story is fundamentally the story of how mammals came to rule the world.
